NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that application is intended to be made to Parliament in the ensuing Session, by the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington, in the respective counties of Lancaster and Chester, (hereinafter called the Cor- poration), for an Act for all or some of the following purposes, that is to say.

To confer in the Corporation powers to Purchase and hold and to enable the Warrington Gas Light and Coke Company (hereinafter called the Company), to sell and transfer to the Corporation the undertaking lands, buildings, works, mains, pipes, approaches, easements, powers, rights, and privileges of or belong- ing to, or possessed or enjoyed by the Company, and for that purpose to conform or give effect, subject to the approval of Parliament, to the provisions of an agreement dated the Twentieth day of October, 1876, and made between the Company of the one part, and the Corporation of the other part. To provide for the dissolution and winding up of the Company, and the distribution of the purchase money or annuities, and the assets of the Company among the several persons entitled thereto.
And the intended Act will confer upon the Corpora. tion the following or some of ;the following powers,

- namely To supply Gas for public and private purposes' and otherwise carry on the undertaking of the Com- pany throughout the limits of supply of the Com- pany. To maintain, re-build, enlarge and repair on the i lands specified n the schedule to the Warrington Gas Act, 1871, and whioh are situate in the borough of Warrington, in the comity of Lancaster, and bounded on the North-East by Academy-street, on the North- West by Chrimes'-yard, and a house and yard late in the occupation of Mr. Fairclough, but now of the Con. servative Club, on the South- West by Lower Bank- street and Upper Bank-street, and on the South-East by Mersey-street, and contain in the whole four acres little more or less, gas works, gasometers, retorts, ma- chinery, apparatus, buildings, approaches works, and conveniences, and to manufacture and :tore gas and the several matters producible from the residual pro. ducts arising or resulting from the manufacture of gas, and also from time to time to purchase by agree- ment, or take on lease, and hold such other lands and property as they may find necessary for the storage of gas, or other purposes of the intended Act.

TO convert, manufacture, sell and dispose of coke, coal, tar, and other residual products arising from the manufacture of gas; and to manufacture, purchase, Bell, and let meters, fittings, and other apparatus, and to make contracts with any persons, companies, or corporations in relation thereto. To lay down and maintain gas, mains, pipes, cul- verts, tramways. and other works in, through, under, over, or across, aid for such purposes to cross, break up, alter, divert, orstop up either temporarily or perma- nently roads, streets, highway, footpaths, and other pub. lie places, bridges, canals, railways, tramways, sewers, drains, streams, brook., water courses, and pipes, and to remove and alter telegraph wires throughout the limits of supply of the Company.

To apply to the purposes of the intended Act, or any of them, any funds or money belonging or coming to them' or which they are or may be empowered to raise by rates, or otherwise under any publio general or other Acts for the time being in force, and to borrow further money for such purposes 011 the credit of their gas undertaking, and of the rates, rents, and charges which they are now authorised to make and levy, or may by the intended Act be authorised to make and levy, and to charge upon the rates, rents, and charges, or any ef them, the payments to be made for the pur- chase forthe gasundertaking, andto snake provision for consolidating the sinking fund in respect of the monies I now owing by the Corporation, with that provided to be borrowed under the intended Act. To make, levy, and recover rates, rents, assessments, and other charges for the supply of gas and the sale and hire of meters and fittings, and other the purposes of the intended Act, and to increase, alter, repeal, or extinguish existing rates, rents, assessments, and charges, and to make new or increased rates, rents, assessments, and charges in lieu thereof, and to grant exemptions from rates, rents, assessments, and charges, and to compound with the owners and occupiers of houses and premises for the payment of such rates, rents, assessments and charges.

To enter into and carry into effect contracts and arrangements for the supply of gas with any 'Urban or other Sanitary or Local Authority, or the Trustees of any turnpike or other road, or any Highway Board, or any Surveyors of any highway, or Company bodies, or persons within or outside the limits of supply of the Company; and the intended Act will confer all neces- sary powers in that behalf upon all such authorities, companies, trustees, bodies, and persons, and will en- able them to apply for the purposes of any such con- tract or arrangements any funds or moneys belonging to them, respectively, or under their control, and to raise money by rates or borrowing. To provide for the payment by the Corporation of all costs, charges and expenses of and incident to the preparing for obtaining and passing the intended Act or otherwise in relation thereto. The intended Act will incorporate with or without variation, and extend and apply to the purposes there- of, all or some of the powers and provisions of "The Gee Works Clauses Act, 1847," And " The Gas Works Clauses Act, 1871." The intended Act will also incorporate and apply to the Corporation, or alter, amend, or appeal so far as may be necessary the provisions of " The Warrington Gas Act, 1847:, The Warrington Gas Act, 1871," " The Warrington Improvement and Market Act, 1864," and of the several "Public Health and Local Government Ads and Local Loans Act," and it will alter' Irary, or extinguish all rights and privileges which would impede or interfere with any of the ob- jects aforesaid, and confer other powers, rights, and privileges. Printed copies of the Bill for the intended Act will be deposited in the Private Bill Office of the House of Commons, on or before the 21st day of December, 1876. div.p: NOXIOUS VAPOURS FROM CHEMICAL WORKS. T. E STATE OF WIDNES, RUNCORN, ST. BELENS, &c. &c.

On Thursday afterne ce a meet'ng was held in the Council Chamber of the T 07711 Halt, Kirig-street, Man- ( heater, with the object of forming in Manchester a branch of the Lanceshire and Cheshire Asrociation for controlling the t scape of Noxious Vepours; and kluide from Manufactories. The Association tcok form in Warrineton about two years ago, and Mr. W. Bea- mont, of that town, and Mr. R. Holland, of Runcorn, attended to explain the course of action which the Asscci ;lion has ursued.—The chair was occupied by the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Curtis.) Mr. DEAMONT said that until the year 1825 there wae a heavy tax On salt, and up to that time the alkali manufacturers of this country were obliged to have re- course to seaside kelp, which wakused with potash imported from America, to make soda. With the abolition of the tax salt came to be used instead of kelp, and Mr. Muspratt, a most enterptising and Spirited men, against whom he did not wieh to say a word, began the manufacture of soda from salt at Liverpool. Mr. Muspratt event on with the manufac- ture in Liverpool until it was found to be such an in. I tolerable nuisance that the Town Council were obliged to proceed against him and he was driven from the town. He then went to Newt= in this county, where he set up new works; but there again the manu- facture was found to be perfectly intolerable, and in the course of the years 18474 an action was instituted against him by the Rector of Winwick (Mr. Hornby) for causing the destruction of a great portion of the timber on his neighbouring estate. Mr. Hernby re- covered from Mr. Mnapratt the sum of £1,250, but Mr. Muspratt could afford to pay and he went on with his works as before In a few years another action wee lodged against him by Mr. Hornby, and that being followed by proceedings on the part of another land- owner, Mr. Muspratt took dow is his works, and &bent 1851 set up others at Widnes. The works grew in number, and in 1883, immense damage having been tione, Lord Derby obtained an act of Parliament patting such works uuder inepeotion. Inspectors care appointed under the Act to see that the works did no damage, but for some reason it was then thought sufficient to limit the oischarge of gases through the chimneys of the works, and nothing wee done to en- force the proper construction of works. It was enacted that not more than five per cent, of muriatic acid should he allowed to escape in that way, and the inspectors took it for granted that all they had to do was to enforce that provision by applying the tests which were directed to the chimneys. On that point Lord Aberdare held a different opinion. The trade was so lucrative that many persons went into it who had not saffiteent capital, and who constructed their Works improperly, and so great evils arose. He was bound to say of many of the manufacturers that they would do anything if they could get rid of the nuisance, but t ere were (Auer men who were engaged in the trade who were hardly so rightly inclined. There Were however, means by which the manufacture of chemicals coul I be conducted without causing harm, and it was the object of the Association of which he Was chairman to get those means put into use. The Association in 1873 drew up a petition on the subject and presented it to the Government. and he believed if it had not happened that there then came a change of Government, Mr. Stansfeld had became so fully alive to the evils they complained of that he was pre- pared to bring in a bill that would have been much More extensive in its scope than any which had yet passed the Legislature. He (the Bleaker) wrote to Mr. Stansfeld after he had retired from office, and he took great penis to insert some clauses which the Mao- dation were anxious should become law into a new bill. In 1873 the Association was busy at work petitioning Parliament and in sending up deputation after deputation to try to influence the Government, and in 1874 the making of copper by the wet process was for the first time included in the Alkali Act. Unfortunately copper-making by the dry process, which was most offensive and deleterious, Beneing off as it did arsenious acids and sulphurous acid, was ex- cluded from the Act. It was one of the objects of the Association to get that process included in the Act, but they were unsuccesefuli After trying in vain to get a further Act of Parliament or an amendment of the Act of 1874 they sought to obtain a Royal Commission, to investigate the subject, and, as everybody knew, that Commission had been sitting in Liverpool. He could assure the meeting that the evidence given by every clam of witnesses before the Commission was to the Association most satisfactory. Among the wa- xiest es were 12 of the most eminent men in Liver- pool—capitalists of all kinds, and every one of them gave evidence of the most convincing character as to great damage which was being done by the chemical works in the south-western portion of the county. They had al-o the evidence of most in- telligent farmers in his district of the damage which they suffered, given in a way that the Commissioners could not possibly resist ; and gentlemen from the east side of Liverpool, where the damage ought to be less, spoke of the effect of the pestiferous blast in their neightouthood. With regard to himself and others arta natintil• Wgioahnri, ci.nd +rho icl6 She full effects of the west winds from St. Helene and Widnes, it was impossible to say how far the damage would go. He had known farmers who had been Obliged to leave the district because their crops were ruined. There would in a few years hardly be a tree left on his occupation ; the fences were all perishing, and vegetation barely lived. It was not that he per- sonally could not leave his residence, for he could do that; but he thought they ought to consider the poor who were obliged to live in such intolerable odours. (Hear, hear.) There could be no real elevation of the people as long as they lived in filth, and could not find within their reach the beauty of untainted nature. (Hear, hear.) Among many things that the Associa- tion of which he was chairman tried to prove to the Commissioners in Liverpool, the difficulty of obtaining legal remedy for direct damage was one. It wai im- possible to say which of the numerous works at Widnes or St. Helens was the particular one that damaged a man's crops or estate, and at present it was futile to ' take proceedings at law. (Hear, hear.) He believed that if they bad the power to sue anyone of the manu- facturers registered within a limited area—and he did not see why that power shoule not be granted by Par- liament, leaving the person so sued to obtain compen- sation from the other offenders within his radius—the manufacturers themselves would soon check the nuisance. 'Hear, hear.) The 'system of inspection was defective, for it was impossible for an inspector living at Liverpool, and having under his charge a wide district, to know what was done during the night time at Widnes or St. Helens; and it most bo remem- bered that it was in the night time or in the early morn- fog that the nuisance was the worst. (Hear, hear.) With reference to the plea that there was no known Method ot utilising the vapours given off, he might Mention that a firm at Warrington was now selling a sulphate at 3 158. a ton, which was made from refuse that, until the Town Council of the borough intervened, they turned into a brook; and from Swansea he had a report which showed that a firm manufacturing copper by the dry process had so utilieed the sulp- hurous acid, which they not long ago discharged into the air, as to make out ef it a product which sold very profitably. (Hear, hear,) What was being done by those firms could be done by others, and he thought they were not unreasonable in insisting that chemical works abould cease to be a nuisance in the country. (Hear, hear.) At Liverpool the manufacturers at- tempted to show that the injury was done by the coal smoke thrown out, and by the sulphurous acid con- tained in such smoke. div.p: IRON AND STEEL: IMPORTANT lINVE NTION.

Leading gentlemen connected with the North- E astern Railway Company, who were in Cleveland on Tuesday, made a statement of the greatest importance to railway interests, and also to the iron trade throughout the world. It seems now to be certain that the experiments which have been carried on by Mr. Isaac Lowthian Bell, M.P., under the auspices of the North-Bastern Railway Company, and which were some time since hopefully spoken of by the chairman, Mr. Leeman, for the production of a cheap and durable iron rail, have been singularly successful. It is confidently affirmed that iron rails, more durable even than steel rails, can be produced by the new pro- cess at much less cost, and at a price but XI per ton in excess of ordinary iron rails. Considering that steel rails when worn are worth little, and that this new rail will be worth two-thirds of its original value for re-conversion, the long agitated question of iron v. steel would seem to be determined. The value of this discovery to Cleveland will be incalculable, as the large substitution of steel for iron rails has been most dis- astrous to her leading interests.

div.head: "HARROGATE WArER" AT CREWE ?
div.p: "HARROGATE WArER" AT CREWE ?

A few weeks ago a gentleman who had been to Harrogate had the curiosity to try a disused pump, erected by the Nantwich Rural Sanitary Authority, near Crewe, and was surprised to discover that the odour and taste of the water was identical with the Spa water at Harrogate. He immediately communi- cated the intelligence to the people of Crewe and the Sanitary Inspector, and the latter gentleman at once despatched two bottles of the water to Dr. Campbell Brown for analysis. The County 'Analyst has re- turned a detailed report of the waters, in which he states that the ingredients are essentially the same as Harrogate waters. Several remarkable cares have been effected by the use of the waters, and a company is in process of formation to work the Spa. There are probably many disused pumps which could furnish water almost as nauseous and noxious as some of the water to be got at Harrogate. It remains to be seen if the water from the disused pump at Crewe is suffi- ciently buoyant to float the shares of the new company. The public will wait with some curiosity for the details of Dr. Campbell Brown's analysis.

Mr. G. Haines Atwell, medical officer of health to the Board, reported that in the quarter ending Sept. • oth, 1876. 95 births and 60 deaths were registered in , the towhehip of Altrincham, Riving a birth rate of 38 and a death rate of 20 per 1,000. 01 the 60 deaths , twelve, or about 25 per cent. were referred to the . seven principal zymotio or infectious diseases, namely, scarlatina 1, diptheria 1, whooping cough 1, diarrheas 9. Besides these, there were 4 deaths from croup, and 2 from puerperal fevers. The one death from scarla- tina occurred in Lloyd's Hospital, where it had been removed from a neighbouring township, and so might be excluded from the semiotic: rate of Altrincham. Excluding this cue, they had 11 deaths from these diseases—about the average of the corresponding quarter for the previous three years. The nine deaths from diarrhoea were about the average also for the corresponding quarters; all, except one of 76 years, were under two years of age, seven being under one year, rind four of these under three months. From the other zymotic diseases there were six deaths, viz., two from puerperal causes, occurring at distant intervals and not apparently in any way con- nected; but the sudden outbreak of croup in the month of August was somewhat remarkable, four deaths being referred to that cause from the 22nd to the 31st, besides one referred to diphtheria and croup; three of these—two of croup—and the one of diph- theria and croup—occurred en the 22nd, two others . following on the 28th and 31st. As these two diseases were sometimes intimately connected, it appeared very probable that the other cases might have had a diphtheritic origin. The mortality among children had been decidedly high, as it generally was during the diarrf ma season; but even that hardly accounted for a somewhat exceptionally high proportion of such deaths. Of the 60 deaths, 25 were under five years of age, 16 of these being under one year, and 12 under three months ; however, 5 of these died within a few hours of congenital defects or weakness, and the others mostly from diarrLosa and original constitu- tional debility. The deaths from croup and diphtheria occurred between one and five years, and were some- what scattered about the township, two occurring in Victoria-street, one in Oakfield-road, one in Police- street, and one in Lloyd-street ; three of these cases, curious enough, happened on one day—the 22nd of August ; all were cases of short duration, except one who had been ill ten days of diphtheria; the other two deaths did not occur until the 28th and 30th of August. With these exceptions, the township• had been very free from the graver forms of epidemic dis- ease. One case of typhoid fever came to his know- ledge, having been contracted evidently while in service at Stretford in a house where a child was ill with fever; this case was removed to Lloyd's Hos- pital, and no further cases occurred in the neighbour- hood tojhis knowledge. THE ALTRINCHAM LOCAL BOARD AND THE RATEPAYERS' REQUISITION. To THE EDITOR OF TEM EXABEIsrnn. Sir,—A question involving an important principle was brought under the notice of the Altrinoham Local Beard, last week. A requisition from a number of pro- perty owners and ratepayers (some fifteen was read) called upon the chairman (Ur. Ghaskarth), to convene a meeting of the ratepayers so that they might express their opinion in regard to purchase of land in Shaw's. lane, Altrincham, for a site for a new market. The Chairman declined to accede to the prayer of the me- morialists on the ground that any other course would ;stultify the acts of the Board with respect to the mar- ket question, which had been adjourned sine die. Another member of the Board, Mr. Barratt, attributed to the memorialists personal interests, whichthe signa- tures it contained would seem to a certain extent to justify. I fancy that it is quite competent for the tatepayers to re-open any question at any time, and the i principle which appears to be involved n this case is, can the Board decline to convene a meeting, on the plea that it would stultify its Own acts F Had the Board refused the request on the ground that the peti- tion was not numerously signed, or wa„ not influential then I could have understood its decision, although I It was might not have entirely approved of it. ad- mitted by the members of the re —"td that bad the memorial been signed by half the - -nhe bi- tants, probably it might have met with a different reciption, quite irrespective of the stultitleu.. tion of the boArd. Tnis argurnentum absurdum was ex- posed by Mr. Burgess who pointed out the preposterous nature of such a thecry. Whoever heard of half a town petitioning any /layer or other official, to con- vene a meeting on any subject? True it was stated that the petitioners could call a meeting themselves, which I presume is the prescriptive right of every Englishman, lout in that case they would have to bear the expense of such an act—although in common with their ratepayers they would only reap the same advan- tages or disadvantages, arising from any decision on the Market question. Any attempt taojosrtiiiflyerutohsfe atah ex- pression of public opinion can only lead to t misgiving, and although, perhaps members of the L3cal Board, don't see the necessi or wisdom of a particular course, yet even the Bugg tion of a handful of their constituents, entitled to consideration, and if possible, adoption. THE METHODIST INEW CONNEXION CHAPEL, ALTRINCHAM.

The annual tea party of the members of this diaper and their friends, took place on Monday evening in the Schoolroom. There was a large attendance, and the room which had been decorated with Rowers and plants, had a very pleasing appearance. Amongst those present there were Mr. J. Rhodes, Brooklauds, the Rev. W. F. Newsans, hey. Mr. Robinson, Rev. T. Scowbv, the Rev. 3. Aylard, /co. &O. After tea the proceedings commenced by the Rev. T. Scowby, giving a description of the state of the church. Although there had not been many accessions, there had been many signs of improvement. Their congregations were very much larger last winter 6than they had been for many winters previously, especially during the evenings. (Hear, hear.) As regarded finances, there was a deficiency, he could not tell how much precisely. but at any rate there was a society debt—and he won- dered if ever there was a Methodist Church which had not one I? He trusted that this would be diminished shortly, and he trusted also that the spirit of liberality would be made manifest amongst their people, and that they would embrace the privilege of giving their sub- stance unto the Lord. Tnere was also another matter. There was not only a debt on the society, but upon that chapel. He tnought it would be a great blessing if that one feature of their chapel were taken away. Their friends were disposed to do that, an effort had been already inaugurated, and he should like that meeting to give some little impetus to the movement. THE RUNCORN GUARDIANS AND MATRIMONY.

A very pleasant termination to an amusing episode of workhouse life transpired at the fortnightly meet- _ lug of the Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday. It will be remembered that some time ago a painter belonging to Runcorn took up his temporary abode in the Woikhouse through a severe attack of illness, and when he was convalescent, anxious to requite the Guardians for their hospitality, he devoted his energies to painting and beautifying the house, the skilful char- actepof his work not only eliciting the admiration of his entertainers, but amply repaying them for their hospi- tality. It was during his painting expedition that the guardians in return for his services found him a wife. He saw, loved, and conquered the heart of a widow, who with her four fatherless children had also made the workhouse her home, and when leaving the hos- pitable establishment, applied for permission—the guardians being loco parentis —to marry the widow, to which their consent was readily granted. A difficulty however, stood in the way—the want of funds—and to obviate this a generous guardian, who was also a clegyman, offered to perform the marriage ceremony for nothing, an offer which was immediately accepted. The prospect, however, was still a dark one, for the bride brought no dowry, except her four children, and the bridegroom was entirely destitute of the needful, so the generous guardians again came to the rescue, making the newly-wedded pair a present of £2 10s. to commence housekeeping with, the money being paid out of the interest fund, On the matter coming to the ears of the Local Government Board, they with their usual official hard heartedness surcharged the treasurer with that amount, on the authority of the auditor, but upon the case being represented to them in a proper light, their hard hearts thawed, and a letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that the circumstances under which the money was paid were "equitable and just," therefore it would be allowed.

WALKING FEAT BY A WIDNES MAN.

During the past week, at the Fair ;Ground, St. Helens, Walter Biggs, of Widnes, has been attempting a great feat in walking. At 11.58 on Tuesday night he commenced the task of walking 350 miles in four days. By 10.66 p.m. on Wednesday he had covered 102 miles and four laps (eleven to the mile), and, although he had very bad weather to contend against, especially on Friday night, he pegged away and com- pleted his 300th mile at 8.28 on Saturday night, the last mile being done in the very fast time of 8 minutes 28 seconds. or considerably less than the fastest time of either Weston or O'Leary. However, the exertion required to do this mile completely exhausted him, and when time was up he had only added about half a dozen to the 300 miles. Messrs. F. W Forster and A. Cox, of Liverpool, both of whom dui:dated in the O'Leary and Weston matches in Liverpool, were timekeepers. _ -

div.head: WIDNES SHOOTING CASE.
div.p: THE WIDNES SHOOTING CASE.

At the Kirkdale Quarter Sessions on Monday, Patrick M‘Manns (23), James Blessington (24), Michael Cox (20), Michael Brady (24), John- Morrisey (24, all labourers, and Bartle Falland (28), chemists' fore- man, were charged with having, at Widnes, on the 7th October, maliciously wounded Thomas Eclleston, The case for the prosecution was that the prisoners. with others, assembledin Major Cross-street, Widnes, on the night reterred to, and assaulted those passing by. While the prosecutor was passing he was knocked down by one of the prisoners, and whilst on the ground he was kicked by several of the others. On getting up and running away some shots were fired after him from a revolver. The prosecutor was not injured by the shots, but a boy was hurt in the foot. The pro- secutor said that the revolver was discharged by Mar- risey, but it was stated by other witnesses that a man not in custody fired the shots. For the defence wit- nesses were called to show that Morrisey was in his house at the time of the occurrence, and that Falland took no part in the affair. It was urged ou behalf of the other prisoners that if they had been guilty of any- thing it was only a common assault; the whole oc- currence being a street brawl. Falland and Morrisey were acquitted. The others were found guilty. Bles- sington was sentenced to twelve months' imprison- ment, and Lt‘Menns, Cox, and Brady were each sen- tenced to nine months' imprisonment.

div.head: MR. SECRETARY CROSS.
div.p: MR. SECRETARY CROSS.

WHEN Mr. Cross awoke one morning and found himself not famous, but Secretary of State for the Home Department, he, like the prophet Ezekiel, was "astonished one hour." His intimate friends and acquaintance were equally astonished for they were ignorant of qualities possessed by their friend, which the genius of Mr. Disraeli had discerned. His townsmen shared in the wonderment. They had been entertaining for several years a future cabinet minister unawares, They thought they had in their midst some score of men quite as able, and perhaps half a dozen much abler. They first had known him as a fifth-rate banister, engaged in an unavailing struggle for briefs, whose industry might some day be rewarded by a County Court Judgeship, and twelve hundred a year; then as a banker thrust in- to the position by an accident, and occupy- ing it as well as could be expected from one fresh to the business and ignorant of it. Suddenly we heard that this highly-respec- table and common-place gentleman was a cabinet minister and Secretary of State! "All the world wondered."

The performances of Mr. Cross as a minis- ter have not belied his antecedents. There has been no conflagration of the Thames, and nobody expected that there would be. The legislation for which he is directly respon- Bible has been of the most meagre and simple description. It has really consisted in giving the drinking portion of the community half- an-hour a day more time to get drunk in, and the factory population half-an-hour a day less time to work in with a corresponding reduction of wages. By one Act he has fostered the vice which is sapping the pros- perity of the nation, and by the other he has probably given the coup de grace to an indus- try already tottering to its fall. If the next generation Bees the great cotton trade of the country a thing of the past like the West India and other trades which have had their day and have vanished, the present Home Secretary will have done his little best to bring about that catastrophe. Of the Artizan Dwellings Act, it is too soon to speak. It will be quite time enough to speak of it as a succese or a failure when some community has tried it. Perhaps we may hear in a few weeks if the Birmingham Corporation have found it of any use in their street reforms. We donot speak either of the Act affecting contracts between masters and servants. Whatever there is in that Act that is effective and creditable belongs to Mr. Lowe, not,to Mr. Cross. We do not re- member anything else that is said to have rendered Mr. Cross's tenure of the Home Office remarkable, except that he has hanged more people recommended to mercy than any of his predecessors. Half a dozen murderers may have come to a just and un- timely end whose ,lives might under other circumstances have been spared. Still while this is a matter of the highest interest to in- dividuals, it is happily of no national im- portance, and the historian of the Disraeli. tish Government will probably spend little time in discussing the question whether or not Mr. Cross deserved the appellation of the "hanging Secretary." Mr. Cross seems to be thought a safe man to send through the country to defend the Ministry in their present difficulties. He has been at Glasgow, and at Man- chester, and he is going to Birmingham. At Glasgow he said nothing, at Manchester he had better have said nothing, and we shall see what he will say at Birming- ham. He has thought it incumbent upon him —holding a Government brief—to get up the Eastern Question, about which he was profoundly ignorant a month ago. Having done so, he has achieved the distinction of having made the very worst speech upon the subject yet made by any man of eminence. His trea'ment of the question at Manches- ter was altogether superficial and shallow. He sprawled over it. He had evidently taken as his text books the speeches and despatches of Lord Derby, and it is amusing by the way to note through his speech the true Lancashire toadyism of the master of Knowsley. As Lord Derby said—as Lord Derby very truly remarked—as Lord Derby very properly put it—as Lord Derby very judiciously observed—this is the burden of the song. Now, Mr. Cross does not know that in appropriating Lord Derby's foreign policy he is a receiver of stolen goods, every- body but himself knowing them to be stolen. Lord Derby never had a policy that he did not steal from somebody. He is a political kleptomaniac. He cannot help stealing. Twelve years ago his policy on the Eastern question was stolen from John Bright. More recently he pilfered from Lord Palmerston. Still later, adopt- ing the Turkish proposal for a six months' armistice instead of his own for six weeks, he stole his policy from the Turks. It is not impossible that a man who appropri- ates—" the wise convey it call "—every policy may settle down upon honesty as the best, in which case the head of the magis- tracy of England may very properly follow

Some few weeks ago there was an article in one of the London papers on the career of the present Ministry. It was in one of those clever journals, the conductors of which believe that they are read out of Lon- don, and have some influence in moulding public opinion out of the metropolis. The article was not favourable, but it said that the only Minister who had redeemed the Govern- ment from unmitigated condemnation was the Home Secretary. If, three years ago, any man who knew Mr. Cross had foretold that England would have been ruled by a Ministry that had been saved from universal contempt by the presence in it of the present Horne Secretary, he would have been "laughed to :.'9orn."

The Servian soldiers exhibit a determination to run away from their enemies which is quite remark- able. The Ifanchester Examiner and Times of yes- terday says :—"Referring to the difficulty of getting the Servian troops to fight, a correspondent at Bel- grade declares that during the engagement on Sun- day some of the Russian officers made use of their revolvers and shot several of the runaways dead on the spot; but even this summary method of dealing with them had no very appreciable effect in staying their flight." That shooting a man dead on the spot should have no appreciable effect in staying his flight is curious, and shows an obstinate perseverance in a vicious course that is very deplorable. And there does not seem to be any good in running away after one is shot dead. The worst would ap- pear to have happened. As regards the future, too, nothing can come of it. He who is shot dead will never live to fight another day however fast and far he may run afterwards. It is altogether an unsatis- factory and illogical habit, and it is to be hoped the Berrien troops will not persist in it. zkr.

THE ARMISTICE: THE CONFERENCE: THE ENGLISH ENVOY.

What may be termed the event of the week is probably the selection of Lord Salisbury to represent Eng- land at the approaching Conference on the Eastern question. The appointment ap- pears to be generally regarded with favour as representing the choice of perhaps the strongest man in the present Cabinet to occupy, practically the place of the English Government at the great European Council which will presently make its supreme dip- lomatic effort to bring about a pacific solu- tion of the Eastern difficulty. The fact of Lord Salisbury's appointment renders needless the statement that the holding of a Conference is definitively settled Turkey, it appears, does not object to a con- ference, providing that she is not excluded. Delegates have been appointed by five of the Ureat Powers to settle a line of demar- cation between the hostile armies in Servia. Germany, it is understood, has refused to send a representative, on the ground that he wishes to avoid the slightest appearance of intervention. With regard to the pro- posed Conference, the Berlin correspondent of the Pall Mall Gazette professes to know that it is to assemble at Constantinople, and that the "difficult questions " have been most agreeably arranged. We are told that the question cone ,rning the exclusion or ad- mission of Turkey has been solved by an arrangement entrusting the Ambassadors accredited at Constantinople with the pre- liminary discussion, without Turkey, of the various points to be considered. It is ex- pected that on all vital points an agreement will be effected. "The programme, thus privately settled, will then be formally sub- mitted to a Conference of all the Powers, including Turkey, for ratification." Russian journals state that the Conference will meet at Brussels,

Consgrvative orators at Chester, Crewe, and indeed wherever anybody can be got to listen to them, have, during the past week, deprecated the just and natural indignation of the English people at the monstrous and inhuman barbarities of the Turkish troops. These friends and patrone of the Turk will read with a curious interest the following statement, which shows that the business of depreciating the wrath of the English people is not yet completed. The statement appears in the Daily News of Thuzsday, and is as follows :

Our Special Commissioner in Bulgaria, telegraphing from Philippopolis, gives an account of a brutal out- rage committed by Turks upon a young girl, and says that similar oases are occurring all over the country daily, and that nothing is done to punish the offenders, except on the urgent representations of the British Consul or Mr. Baring, who do not hear of one in a hundred of the crimes which are perpetrated. The girl in question died the following morning as the re- sult of her horrible usage. Lady Strangford has visited Batak, riding all the way on horseback, not- withstanding the rain and cold. In spite of the re- peated promises of the Turks, she did not find that a single house had been rebuilt. The authorities had furnished wood for building, but had done nothing more; and in no part of the country, says our Com- missioner, have they put up a single roof.

This kind of thing must be particularly distressing to the friends of the Ciovernment whose business seems to be to wash the blackam ,or white, and to regard all Turk- ish horrors in a placid and benign spirit.

THE BLAOICHORSE HOTEL AGAIN. At the Presoot Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the case of Mr. Thomas Ingham, of the Black Horse Hotel, Farnworth, again came on for hearing before Mr. S. Thompson and Mr. W. L. Evans. Mr. Stanley Bremner, of Liverpool, again defended, the charge being that the defendant "did unlawfully sell by re- tail intoxicating liquors, without being duly licensed to P ell the same." At the annual licensing session Mr. Ingham's licence was withheld, on the ground of a conviction against him, and notice of appeal was given by Air. Bremner, sen., at the time. On the 13th nit.. Inspector Barnett visited the defendant's house and found persons drinking there, and paying for what was supplied to them. The police officer asked on what authority the defendant was selling, and the latter failed to produce any authority. The matter was brought into court, and the case adjourned for the pro- duction of the "order" from the Board of Inland Re- venue, "permitting a person, whose licence was refused to carry on business durieg the pendency of an appeal, under the 63rd section of the licensing aots. Mr. - Bremner now explained that owing to some inadver- tence the "order" had not been received at the time the polioe-ofacer called, but that he would now cell the chief-officer of Excise, who would produce the receipt ' for the money. Mr. Spencely, magistrates' clerk, in- timated that the receipt had already been produced, and asked if there was any order. Mr. Bremner said there was, and a document was handed to Mr. Spencely who said it was simply an order of the board to their officer to take certain money. It was not an order for permission to sell, as required by the act, and it seemed clear that the board had not yet had sufficient practice in making out such orders to do it properly. He did not know whether that was the usual way in which the Excise did their business. Mr. Bremner Might I suggest to the police that the information be with. ? Mr. Brindle, the police superintendent, left the matter in the hands of the magistrates. Mr. Ing- ham having hid his licence restored at Kirkdale Quarter Sessions, the magistrates eventually decided to dismiss the case.

FOREIGN NEWS. FRANCE. • THE PROSECUTION OF COMMUNISTS:, In the French Chamber the Bill potting an end to further prosecutions of the Communists was adopted on Saturday in an amended fo, m. The bitl provides that from the date of its promulgation no prosecutions are to take place, except for murder, arson, and robbery. All judiclal proceedings commenced but not yet terminated are to be dtopped. Charges of murder, arsbn aid robbery are henceforth to be tried by jell instead of court-martial. ITALY. DEATH OF THE POPE'S PRIME MINISTER. From Rome the death was announced on Monday of the famous Papal statesman, Cardinal Antouelli. The deceased was born in April, 1806, and was consequently in his 71st year. He was the son of humble parents in the Campagna, and entered the Church at an early. age. Soon attracting the notice of Pope G-egory XVI., he was appointed to several responsible duces under that Pontiff. On the accession of Pius IX. his good fortune con!'nued. He was made a cardinal, and became the principal Minister of the Papal aivernd ment. This position he may be said to have held until the overthrow of the Temporal Power in 1870. After that event his influence with the Pope declined. and he ceased to play a conspicuous part in public affairs.
